His 92.8 mph average exit velocity sits in the 96th percentile, his 50.3% hard-hit rate matches his xSLG of .498, and the .365 xwOBA says the production is already there in the batted-ball data even before a full season of it compounds. The one genuine tension in the profile is the glove: a 1st-percentile OAA figure at third base means Tampa is carrying real defensive cost to keep his bat in the lineup every day. If the bat does what the contact metrics say it can, that cost is worth paying for a middle-of-the-order force who also draws an 11.8% walk rate; if the defense forces a move to DH, the offensive ceiling stays intact but the roster flexibility shrinks considerably.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA and hard-hit rate tell one story; the strikeout rate tells another. Crow-Armstrong's .359 xwOBA and 49.0% hard-hit rate sit in the top tier of contact quality, yet a 26.8% K% and 34.1% chase rate are the drag weights pulling actual results below what the batted-ball profile earns. The walk rate, 12.0% and well above a typical hacker's, is what keeps the equation solvent, because a hitter chasing that much who also draws walks is threading a needle, and the projection trusts he keeps threading it: .274/.368/.538 with 38 home runs and 38 stolen bases across 714 plate appearances. Everything hinges on whether the discipline holds, because if the chase rate climbs and the walks dry up, the power plays smaller fast.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .304 with a 100th-percentile mark, the xwOBA at .383, and neither figure is a quirk of the park or the schedule — a 92.5 mph average exit velo and 51.4% hard-hit rate say the contact quality is genuine and consistent. The one real tension in the profile is discipline: a 33.2% chase rate trails most hitters with this kind of bat-to-ball ceiling, and if pitchers ever solve him with secondary stuff away, the walk rate and average both soften together. What the projection translates to is a .288/.362/.470 line with 40 steals in 629 plate appearances, which is a perennial MVP-conversation player at a premium position, and the 99th-percentile sprint speed makes the stolen-base total conservative rather than ambitious. He is, simply, the player Kansas City is built around.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The power-speed combination is legitimate and the contact profile is what it is. A 92.6 mph average exit velocity with a 13.7% barrel rate explains the .490 xSLG, and at 29.2 ft/s he's a genuine base-stealing threat. The catch is a 35.8% chase rate that pitchers have already found and will keep finding, which is why the whiff rate sits at 30.6% and the walk rate is a modest 7.8%. If the swing decisions don't sharpen, the .344 OBP in the projection stays a ceiling rather than a floor, and the whole profile leans on his batted-ball quality carrying him through the contact inefficiency. But 32 home runs and 20 steals in 672 projected plate appearances is a legitimate fantasy anchor at 24, and the Statcast contact markers are good enough that he earns the benefit of the doubt on whether the raw does enough to offset the chase.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA tells two separate stories here, .409 with the bat and .257 against hitters on the mound, and both land in the 94th percentile or better. That split is the whole argument: contact quality this elite on both sides of the ball, sustained across a real sample, doesn't happen by accident. The 16.6% barrel rate as a hitter is among the loudest in baseball, and a 2.72 xERA with a 30.4% whiff rate as a pitcher describes a genuine frontline arm, not a novelty act. The projection's .943 OPS across 691 plate appearances feels conservative given those underlying numbers, and the profile hinges entirely on staying healthy enough to log meaningful innings in both roles, because the floor without the mound is still an elite DH and the floor without the bat is still a staff ace.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 1.99 xERA with a 39.3% strikeout rate isn't a profile you round off — it's the kind of Statcast card that makes you check whether you're reading it right. Misiorowski's fastball sits at 100.6 mph with 2634 rpm of spin, which explains the 37.9% whiff rate and the .219 xwOBA against; hitters aren't squaring him up because they genuinely can't locate the ball. The 6.0% walk rate is the one number keeping this from being absurd, and if it drifts back up, the whole thing gets messier fast. If it holds, the projection calls for 265 strikeouts and a 1.97 ERA over 182.2 innings, which stops looking like an error.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-three home runs projected at 22 years old is loud enough on its own, but the Statcast profile is what makes it believable: a 13.2% barrel rate sits in the 87th percentile, and the .470 xSLG tracks almost exactly with what the projection has him doing. The gap between that xSLG and a 38.3% hard-hit rate in the 38th percentile is the puzzle, suggesting the damage comes in concentrated bursts rather than broad contact quality, which is fine until pitchers find a pattern to exploit in his 27.1% whiff rate. If the barrel rate holds as his primary lever, he's a middle-of-the-order corner bat who gives Cincinnati something real; if the whiff creep compounds, you're left with a thump machine who needs careful deployment.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs and 30 steals from a shortstop is a rare combination, and the Statcast profile explains how it's happening without being a pure contact story. The power reads as legitimate at a 10.3% barrel rate with an .xSLG of .446, even though the 89.5 mph average exit velocity is right at the median, because he's generating barrels efficiently rather than just mashing everything hard. What makes him genuinely dangerous is that the projection's .273/.347/.511 line assumes his legs keep doing real work alongside the pop, and at 28.5 ft/s he has the speed to post 30 steals in a full season. The catch in the profile is the 37.2% chase rate, which is a real liability, and if pitchers learn to exploit it more aggressively the strikeouts climb past 23.2% and the walks stay stuck near 8.6%, which puts pressure on everything downstream.

His 12.4% strikeout rate sits in the 93rd percentile, and his 17.8% whiff rate is equally elite — he just doesn't miss, which is why an 87.6 mph average exit velocity and a 4.7% barrel rate still produce a usable .268/.332/.383 projection line over 649 plate appearances. The tension is that his contact game is built on weak-to-medium contact rather than damage, and if pitchers consistently work to his chase rate (37.3%, 12th percentile) and he starts expanding, the strikeout suppression that holds this profile together unravels fast. A second-division regular right now, with a path to more if the plate discipline tightens, and a bench bat waiting if it doesn't.

reports.published_report: A 13.8% strikeout rate at catcher is quietly elite, and that's the number that makes the rest of Contreras's profile click. The contact quality is consistent across the board: a .263 xBA, a .440 xSLG, and a 20.3% whiff rate all clustering in the same upper-quarter range, telling the same story about a hitter who puts the ball in play hard and rarely gets fooled. The projection's .265/.339/.396 line at 641 plate appearances feels like a mild discount on what the Statcast profile suggests he can do, and he'll give it to you from behind the plate. Slow-footed and not a walking machine, but for a catcher this age, the bat-to-ball skill is the axis everything turns on, and his holds up.

reports.name: Charlie Condon
reports.published_report: The ISO is the argument: .246 at AAA in 485 plate appearances, translating to .183 at the MLB level against a pool where that figure is a legitimate separator. Condon is getting to real power, and the 64 walks alongside 22 home runs at AAA show a hitter hunting his pitch rather than swinging through contact, which is what makes the translation believable. The friction is the 25.7% K% the translation carries at the MLB level, and at first base that margin has to be covered by the bat. If it is, he's a low-end everyday regular; if the strikeout rate bites into the power production, you're left with a bench bat who can hurt you on the right pitch.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The profile is a contradiction wrapped in a box score: the contact shapes (.253 xBA, .419 xSLG) suggest a playable everyday hitter, but a 39.1% chase rate that sits near the bottom of the league explains why the xwOBA lands at .314 despite the solid barrel and slug numbers. He chases, he doesn't walk (5.5% BB%), and those two habits compound each other into a projected .296 OBP that turns an 18-HR, 15-SB season into something closer to a second-division regular than an impact bat. At 29.3 ft/s, his sprint speed grades at the 93rd percentile, giving him a margin that most hitters with this contact profile don't have. The whole thing hinges on whether he can tighten the zone: if the chase rate doesn't come down, the .702 projected OPS is the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Brice Turang
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the load-bearing wall. At 12.8% BB%, Turang sits comfortably above most middle infielders, and that discipline is what props a .343 xwOBA onto contact quality that's solid but not spectacular — 90.4 mph average exit velocity, a 7.7% barrel rate, nothing that screams damage on its own. The strikeout rate, 24.8%, is the friction in the profile: he chases just 25.1% of pitches out of the zone, so the whiffs come from something other than aggression, and the projection's .260/.352/.429 line stays healthy only if that walk rate holds. If it regresses toward league-average, the contact numbers aren't loud enough to carry him, and you're looking at a second-division regular rather than a genuinely useful piece; if it holds, 19 home runs and 23 stolen bases at second base is a real everyday player.

reports.name: Nolan McLean
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the card: 27.3 K% puts him well into the top fifth of starters, yet the chase rate sits at a pedestrian 27.9% — he's getting swings and misses without generating a lot of chases outside the zone, which is a combination that tends to be fragile when hitters make adjustments. The 9.1 BB% is the part that keeps this from being a cleaner story; a 3.70 xERA with that walk rate means he's working around more traffic than the surface ERA suggests, and the projection's 3.38 with 177.7 innings leans on the strikeouts suppressing enough damage to cover the control lapses. If the chase rate stays low and the walks stay elevated, what's left is a back-end starter who misses bats in the zone but gives too much away; if the command firms up even modestly, the strikeout volume makes a mid-rotation ceiling real.

reports.name: James Tibbs III
reports.published_report: The .422 OBP and 27 home runs at AAA are doing a lot of work here, but the translation is what makes this interesting. James Tibbs III's walk rate comes out to 13.3% against big-league pitching, nearly five points clear of what the average MLB hitter draws, and his ISO translates to .193, both suggesting the hit tool and power aren't just AAA inflation. The catch is the ceiling: ValuCast has him up +2 in his prospect ranking recently, yet the peak here is a low-end everyday regular, and if the strikeout rate, which translates to 23.4% in the majors, doesn't stabilize, what's left is a patient bench bat at first base. At 23, with 87 walks in 528 AAA plate appearances, the contact/power mix needs to sharpen rather than bloom to get him over that line.

reports.name: Otto Lopez
reports.published_report: A 12.7% strikeout rate with a 5.2% walk rate is a sharp imbalance, and the Statcast card lays out exactly how he survives it. His xBA sits at the 91st percentile because he makes so much contact and puts it in play cleanly, not because he's punishing mistakes — the 6.1% barrel rate and pedestrian exit velocity say he's a singles-and-speed operator who compounds hits rather than creating damage. The projection's .302/.340/.439 line with 30 steals reads as a credible translation of that profile, a player whose floor is something close to an offensive regular and whose ceiling is roughly where the projection lands, so long as the elite contact rate holds at the big-league level and the walk rate doesn't become a liability when pitchers learn to exploit that 32.3% chase rate. Throw in a 96th-percentile OAA mark at the middle infield spots and Lopez is more than the sum of the bat.

reports.name: Parker Messick
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA land at 90th percentile each, and that's the argument in two numbers: Messick suppresses hard contact at a level that explains the results rather than contradicting them. A 5.0% barrel rate and 32.5% hard-hit rate get there without elite swing-and-miss, which is the honest shape of the profile — his 26.1% whiff rate sits in the middle of the league, and the fastball spin at 2173 rpm is a bottom-fifth reading. What he does is locate, miss bats when it counts, and keep barrels off the ball, and the projection's 2.77 ERA over 184.6 innings trusts that formula to hold across a full season.

reports.name: Randy Arozarena
reports.published_report: Quietly average everywhere except where it counts. The Statcast card is a study in respectable middles: exit velo at 90.7 mph, K% and BB% both sitting right at league average, a barrel rate that won't scare anyone. What lifts it is the contact quality relative to results: an xwOBA of .344 and an xBA of .261 suggest the actual bat-to-ball shape is better than the surface lines imply, and a projection of 22 home runs and 25 stolen bases in 659 plate appearances is the kind of dual-threat output that makes a player more valuable than any single number describes. The profile hinges on his legs holding up; if the sprint speed at 27.0 ft/s keeps eroding, the stolen base piece quietly deflates and what's left is a solid, unspectacular corner bat. Right now the two tools together make him a genuine everyday player.

reports.name: Lawrence Butler
reports.published_report: The disconnect between his contact profile and his approach profile is the whole tension here. Butler's chase rate sits at 25.3%, better than three-quarters of the league, and his 11.3% walk rate matches that discipline — yet a 27.2% whiff rate keeps dragging the xBA down to .238, which is where the .220 projection AVG lives. He makes the right decisions outside the zone, then struggles to do damage once he's in it, and the 44.8% hard-hit rate against an xSLG of .379 tells you the contact that does happen isn't consistently loud enough to carry the strikeouts. If the whiff rate comes down inside the zone, the walk rate and approach already in place give him a real offensive floor as a second-division regular with 16 home runs and speed; if it doesn't, he's a useful bench piece whose on-base skills keep him around but whose bat never quite arrives.

reports.published_report: The gap between a 3.55 ERA projection and a 4.20 xERA is the whole argument here. Weathers strikes out 25.4% of hitters and walks only 6.9%, a combination that drives the projection's optimism, but his 29.2% chase rate sits well below league average, which means those strikeouts are coming from hitters swinging at pitches they want rather than pitches they don't — a shakier foundation than the K% alone suggests. The 2473 rpm fastball spin is genuinely loud, yet the 93.7 mph velocity means spin alone isn't generating plus swing-and-miss. A 32.5% strikeout rate and a 2.94 xERA are closer to shutdown-closer territory than to a middle-relief arm, and a 32.6% whiff rate sustained across meaningful MLB exposure says hitters aren't making contact because they can't, not because they're swinging at bad pitches — the 30.4% chase rate is dead average. The 11.6% walk rate is the one number that prevents this from being a cleaner story, sitting near the bottom of the league and pushing the projected WHIP to 1.37 despite quality underlying contact suppression. If he tightens the command, a 3.28 ERA projection starts looking conservative; if he doesn't, the walks eventually find the barrel and the xERA gap closes the wrong way.

reports.name: Charles Davalan
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline profile here is so clean it almost makes you suspicious — 51 strikeouts against 59 walks across 474 plate appearances at A+, with the translated K% sitting at 16.0% while the MLB average sits at 22.0%. That's a legitimate separator, and the .409 OBP with a .247 ISO shows the power translating alongside it, not instead of it. The MLB-equivalent ISO of .163 clears the league mean, which tells you this isn't a slap-happy contact hitter who lucked into a gaudy BABIP, and his .291 BABIP lines up with his .293 average close enough that neither is doing suspicious work. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat with the floor matching it, so the whole profile hinges on whether the contact rates hold against better velocity and spin at higher levels; if they do, you have a usable major-leaguer, and if they don't, the power probably isn't enough to carry him on its own.

reports.name: Sterlin Thompson
reports.published_report: The .461 OBP at AAA is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's built on a real foundation: 55 walks against 49 strikeouts in 293 plate appearances, a walk rate that translates to 13.7% at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer walks at 8.5%. The strikeout translation, 19.6% in MLB context, would play comfortably in the middle of the big-league distribution. What doesn't translate as cleanly is the ISO, .165 at AAA becoming .139 in the MLB equivalent, and that gap is where the ceiling question lives: the hit-and-walk game is genuine, but without more over-the-fence impact, a left-handed corner outfielder who doesn't mash is always auditioning for someone's bench. Either a solid platoon piece or a good bench bat depending on how much that power gap closes against better arms.

reports.name: Vinnie Pasquantino
reports.published_report: The contact profile here is genuinely good, and 13 projected home runs is the tension. A 15.5% whiff rate and 10.9% walk rate place him well above average at both; he's one of the harder first basemen in the league to put away. The problem is that none of it is translating into thump: the Statcast profile has him at .412 xSLG, which is fine but not first-base fine, and the projection lines out at .398 SLG across 484 plate appearances. If the exit velocity (89.5 mph, roughly average) doesn't climb as he recovers health and re-establishes his swing, what's left is a disciplined, light-hitting first baseman, which is a tough roster argument at that position.

reports.name: Jake Bennett

reports.name: Ronny Hernandez
reports.published_report: The plate discipline at A+ is genuinely loud: 37 walks against 33 strikeouts in 232 plate appearances, a 16% walk rate paired with a 14% strikeout rate that translates to roughly league-average contact and above-average patience at the MLB level. The .251 ISO at A+ is the headline, but the translation brings it back to earth at .161, still a tick above a league-average mark of .150, which is where the ceiling argument lives and where the skepticism starts. Everything here hinges on whether that contact quality survives the jump to upper minors, because a 1B profile with a bench-or-platoon ceiling has very little margin if the power thins out two levels up. Right now he's one of the cleaner discipline profiles in this class; two to three years from now he's either a useful left-handed bat off the bench or a guy the system quietly moves on from.

reports.name: Connelly Early
reports.published_report: The gap between a 3.51 ERA projection and a 4.31 xERA is the whole argument here, and it's not an encouraging one. Early's Statcast contact profile is genuinely punishing — a 10.6% barrel rate and 40.9% hard-hit rate both sit well below the median, and hitters are squaring him up consistently enough that the underlying run-prevention math leans toward regression. His 31.4% chase rate gives him something to work with, but a 23.7% whiff rate means he's not finishing those expanded swings at a useful clip. If that chase-to-whiff disconnect holds, he profiles as a back-end rotation filler who gives Washington league-average length on a good day and early showers when his location slips.

reports.name: Marcus Phillips
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the command is the problem, and right now the problem is winning. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Translate that profile to MLB-equivalent and the strikeouts land near league average while the walk rate lands at 6.4, roughly double what big-league starters typically allow, and a K-BB% of 8.6% against the 13.5% norm tells you exactly how much the free passes are eating the upside. The entire profile hinges on whether the walks compress as he matures, because if they don't, the strikeout ceiling has nowhere to go and he's a depth arm by ceiling and floor.

reports.name: Abner Uribe
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells the story cleanly: 1.6% against contact, a figure that sits at the 99th percentile. Pair that with a 99.0 mph fastball and a .260 xwOBA, and you have a reliever who makes hard contact almost impossible even when hitters do connect. The walk rate at 9.4% is the friction point, because the stuff plays elite when he's in counts and falls apart when he starts falling behind, and the 27.9% chase rate suggests he isn't manufacturing outs off the plate when the control slips. If the walks stay in this range, he's a high-leverage bridge arm with closer upside; if they spike, he becomes too volatile for the eighth inning regardless of how good 99 mph looks on the radar gun.

reports.name: Mike Sirota
reports.published_report: The .468 OBP is the headline, but the .399 BABIP behind it is where this profile gets complicated. Across AA & A+, Sirota has walked 91 times against 100 strikeouts in 455 plate appearances, and that discipline translates to a 14.5% walk rate in MLB terms, well above what the average big-leaguer draws at 8.5%. The power translates modestly, a .165 ISO equivalent, which means the ceiling is a patient center fielder who sprays line drives and takes his walks, not a middle-of-the-order bat. If the contact rate holds and he hits something closer to his true average, he's a useful bench or platoon piece with real on-base value; if the BABIP collapses, what's left is the walk rate alone.

reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. reports.name: Ryan Clifford
reports.published_report: Sixteen home runs in 431 AAA plate appearances is the one thing keeping this profile alive. The raw power translates to a .140 ISO at the MLB level, roughly matching what an average big-league hitter produces, but a K% that would run 35.1% in the majors means he'd be striking out at a rate that makes even the power hard to deploy. At AAA this year, he's hitting .175 with a .267 OBP, and a .249 BABIP says the contact isn't hiding behind bad luck. Everything hinges on whether he can make enough contact to let the pop matter, and right now, 164 strikeouts in a single AAA season says he can't.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

Thirty-nine walks in 229 AAA plate appearances, a 17% clip at that level, translates to a 12.3% MLB-equivalent BB%, and the league average sits at 8.5%. The ISO translates to .144, right at the MLB mean, so there's no carry tool here to paper over a rough stretch. If the zone discipline survives the jump and the average stays near its current floor, Schreck is a bench bat with genuine on-base utility; if the approach gets exposed at the MLB level, what's left is a fringe center fielder with league-average power and not much else.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
